subject: appropriate number of items to be used by mirt function for calibration

messages.author: 84aac2580b195c68
messages.subject: appropriate number of items to be used by mirt function for calibration
parts:
Hello Phil,


Is there any limit ( upper and/or lower) on number of items for going together for calibration using mirt() function. What is the optimum number of items should one use at a time for calibration to get the best results?


Does this number change as we change the item type or ( dich or poly) or we change the number of dimensions underlying ?





Thanking you,


Irshad.

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: appropriate number of items to be used by mirt function for calibration
parts:
On Mon, Feb 23, 2015 at 7:41 AM, Irshad Mujawar <irshadmuj...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hello Phil,


Is there any limit ( upper and/or lower) on number of items for going together for calibration using mirt() function. What is the optimum number of items should one use at a time for calibration to get the best results?

I have no idea what this means. Optimal in what sense, measuring individuals precisely, item parameters or group parameters well; and what is meant be 'best' here? The smallest standard error (or a SE < #.... and for which parameters), the least bias, the most robust? The question is way too open ended to form a correct answer.
Does this number change as we change the item type or ( dich or poly) or we change the number of dimensions underlying ?

Yes, and yes. More dimensions generally means that you need more items for everything, and polytomous items behave differently because they generally have more parameters to estimate (but also provide more information, so even that is difficult). But it also depends on the class of items: 1PL need far less subjects compared to the 3PL, and nominal many more than the gpcm. So the big answer to you email, and all statistical models in general, is that it depends on a large number of interacting factors.

Phil
 





Thanking you,


Irshad.

That still is very open ended, and I feel like you are looking for an exact answer when at best I could give arbitrary rules of thumb (which I am vehemently against anyway). My recommendation would be to try simulating data to get a feel for your item bank given the class of IRT models you are using. Try different sample sizes, item bank sizes, etc, and repeat each sample size multiple times to get an idea of how the item parameters vary, especially in regards to the population simulating parameters.

Phil
